idiom_name: @PreAuthorize with an AuthorizationManager/SpEL predicate comparing the approver to the stored initiator
implementation_notes: The default JVM realization: method security puts an interceptor in front of the service bean, reads the authenticated principal from the SecurityContext and evaluates the annotation's SpEL or AuthorizationManager expression, so the separation predicate is a policy expression - the current authentication name differs from the persisted request's initiator and the caller holds the release authority. What replaces the classic role structure is the combination of authorities granted to distinct accounts with this expression; the workflow states and the initiator's identity come from the durable request. Choose it when the application owns its authorization layer and the toolchain is Java 17+ (Spring Security 6); below that floor, or outside Spring, the JAAS realization or an explicit service check is the alternative.
pitfalls: Unannotated methods are unprotected and self-invocation inside the same bean bypasses the proxy - declare a catch-all rule and call secured methods through the proxy (or from another bean).

Identities taken from the request body are attacker-controlled; read the initiator from the persisted record and the approver from the Authentication, and compare stable ids rather than display names.
@PostAuthorize on a method that writes is too late - the write has already happened; authorize before the state transition.

variants.name: JAAS Subject.doAs with distinct Subjects per duty
variants.implementation_notes: The JDK's own model, and the basis of container-managed authorization: authenticate each actor into its own Subject populated with Principals, then run each duty with Subject.doAs(subject, action) so the decision is made for that subject. Separation of duties is expressed by granting the terminal permission only to the checker subject, so a maker subject cannot complete the operation regardless of the code it runs. What replaces the classic role structure is the Subject/Principal pair plus the policy decision; the workflow row still records who initiated and who approved. Choose it where a JAAS-based container is the enforcement point and the toolchain predates Spring Security 6, and note that the java.security.Policy/AccessController permission layer was deprecated for removal by JEP 411 - keep JAAS authentication, move the decision to an explicit check or a modern framework.
pitfalls: Subject.doAs binds the subject to the current thread's AccessControlContext; thread pools and asynchronous continuations lose or leak it unless the subject is captured and restored explicitly.

The java.security.Policy and AccessController permission layer is deprecated for removal (JEP 411); JAAS authentication remains, but building a new enforcement point on the deprecated policy API is a dead end.
Two Subjects for the same physical person (a shared login) is the classic self-approval hole; keep the principal-to-person binding reviewed and audited.
